quotes.text: For putting in chains, for killing, for dragging whither they choose, for taking away what a man has.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Speak of the thing as it is: how strange that the poor body of Socrates should have been carried off and dragged to prison by stronger men, and that anyone should have given hemlock to the poor body of Socrates, and that it should breathe out the life.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Anytus and Melitus can kill me, but they cannot hurt me: and further, he says, “If it so pleases God, so let it be.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But a man has seized me by the cloak, and is drawing me to the public place: then others bawl out, “Philosopher, what has been the use of your opinions?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And what system of philosophy (εἰσαγωγήν) could I have made so that, if a stronger man should have laid hold of my cloak, I should not be dragged off; that if ten men should have laid hold of me and cast me into prison, I should not be cast in?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I have learned to see that everything which happens, if it be independent of my will, is nothing to me.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Why then do you seek advantage in anything else than in that in which you have learned that advantage is?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You will never show this, nor come near showing it; for this is the law of nature and of God that the superior shall always overpower the inferior.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: One body is stronger than another: many are stronger than one: the thief is stronger than he who is not a thief.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But the man bought the lamp at this price: for a lamp he became a thief, a faithless fellow, and like a wild beast.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then sitting in prison I say: The man who cries out in this way neither hears what words mean, nor understands what is said, nor does he care at all to know what philosophers say or what they do.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —If you have no further need of me in prison, I come out: if you should have need of me again, I will enter the prison.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —So long as reason requires me to be with the body: but when reason does not require this, take away the body, and fare you well.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Only we must not do it inconsiderately, nor weakly, nor for any slight reason; for, on the other hand, God does not wish it to be done, and he has need of such a world and such inhabitants in it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if he sounds the signal for retreat, as he did to Socrates, we must obey him who gives the signal, as if he were a general.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When children come clapping their hands and crying out, “Today is the good Saturnalia,” do we say, “The Saturnalia are not good”?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you also then, when you are not able to make a man change his mind, be assured that he is a child, and clap your hands with him; and if you do not choose to do this, keep silent.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: A man must keep this in mind; and when he is called to any such difficulty, he should know that the time is come for showing if he has been instructed.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Even among the gladiators of Caesar (the Emperor) there are some who complain grievously that they are not brought forward and matched, and they offer up prayers to God and address themselves to their superintendents entreating that they may fight.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I would willingly take a voyage for this purpose and see what my athlete is doing, how he is studying his subject.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: There has been given to you such a body as you have, such parents, such brethren, such a country, such a place in your country:—then you come to me and say, “Change my subject.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: However, you do not say so, but you say, “Do not propose to me such a tropic, but such : do not urge against me such an objection, but such .”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For he who is come into a difficulty is like a young man from a school who has practiced the resolution of syllogisms; and if any person proposes to him an easy syllogism, he says: rather propose to me a syllogism which is skillfully complicated that I may exercise myself on it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: There will be a time perhaps when tragic actors will suppose that they are masks and buskins and the long cloak.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Utter something that we may know whether you are a tragic actor or a buffoon; for both of you have all the rest in common.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If anyone then should take away the tragic actor’s buskins and his mask, and introduce him on the stage as a phantom, is the tragic actor lost, or does he still remain?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: ; but when the time of trial is come, one of you must weep and say, “I wish that I had learned more.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I think that there is someone, among you who are sitting here, who is suffering like a woman in labor, and saying, “Oh, that such a difficulty does not present itself to me as that which has come to this man; oh, that I should be wasting my life in a corner, when I might be crowned at Olympia.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For when Vespasian sent and commanded him not to go into the senate, he replied, “It is in your power not to allow me to be a member of the senate, but so long as I am, I must go in.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You will do your part, and I will do mine: it is your part to kill; it is mine to die, but not in fear: yours to banish me; mine to depart without sorrow.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —I am in a wretched condition, Master (Lord), and I am unfortunate; no man cares for me, no man gives me anything; all blame me, all steak ill of me.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —Is this the evidence that you are going to give, and disgrace his summons, who has conferred so much honor on you, and thought you worthy of being called to bear such testimony?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: “Lay aside the laticlave (the mark of senatorial rank), and clothing yourself in rags, come forward in this character.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What then, have I not the power of displaying a good voice (that is, of doing something that I ought to do)?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: “Come forward, you, and bear testimony for me, for you are worthy to be brought forward as a witness by me: is anything external to the will good or bad?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then is it the fact that a musician pays no regard to him who declares that the lowest chord in the lyre is the highest; nor yet a geometrician, if he declares that the lines from the centre of a circle to the circumference are not equal; and shall he who is really instructed pay any regard to the uninstructed man when he pronounces judgment on what is pious and what is impious, on what is just and unjust?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if the same person had passed judgment on a hypothetical syllogism (συνημμένου), and had made a declaration, “the conclusion that, if it is day, it is light, I declare to be false,” what has happened to the hypothetical syllogism?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Will you not leave the small arguments (λογάρια) about these matters to others, to lazy fellows, that they may sit in a corner and receive their sorry pay, or grumble that no one gives them anything; and will you not come forward and make use of what you have learned?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For it is not these small arguments that are wanted now: the writings of the Stoics are full of them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Assume, I entreat you, this character, that we may no longer use in the schools the examples of the ancients, but may have some example of our own.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if I shall release myself from my masters, that is from those things by means of which masters are formidable, what further trouble have I, what master have I still?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But it is shameful to contemplate these things as runaway slaves do: we should sit, as in a theatre, free from distraction, and listen at one time to the tragic actor, at another time to the lute-player; and not do as slaves do.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As soon as the slave has taken his station he praises the actor and at the same time looks round: then if anyone calls out his master’s name, the slave is immediately frightened and disturbed.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Man is not the master of man; but death is, and life and pleasure and pain; for if he comes without these things, bring Caesar to me and you will see how firm I am.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But when he shall come with these things, thundering and lightning, and when I am afraid of them, what do I do then except to recognize my master like the runaway slave?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But so long as I have any respite from these terrors, as a runaway slave stands in the theatre, so do I: I bathe, I drink, I sing; but all this I do with terror and uneasiness.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No, but we ought to accommodate ourselves to the ignorant (τοῖς ἰδιώταις) and to say: “This man recommends to me that which he thinks good for himself: I excuse him.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For Socrates also excused the jailor, who had the charge of him in prison and was weeping when Socrates was going to drink the poison, and said, “How generously he laments over us.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No, but he says it to his friends who were able to hear (understand) it; and he treats the jailor as a child.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When you are going in to any great personage, remember that another also from above sees what is going on, and that you ought to please him rather than the other.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: He then who sees from above asks you: “In the schools what used you to say about exile and bonds and death and disgrace?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then go in to the great personage boldly and remember these things; and you will see what a youth is who has studied these things when he is among men who have not studied them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I indeed imagine that you will have such thoughts as these: Why do we make so great and so many preparations for nothing?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Why, what else than this, that it is conspicuous in the toga as purple, and is displayed also as a fine example to all other things?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But in such circumstances another would have replied to Caesar who forbade him to enter the senate, “I thank you for sparing me.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But such a man Vespasian would not even have forbidden to enter the senate, for he knew that he would either sit there like an earthen vessel, or, if he spoke, he would say what Caesar wished, and add even more.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In this way an athlete also acted who was in danger of dying unless his private parts were amputated.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: His brother came to the athlete, who was a philosopher, and said, “Come, brother, what are you going to do?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As a man, Epictetus replied, and a man who had been proclaimed among the athletes at the Olympic games and had contended in them, a man who had been familiar with such a place, and not merely anointed in Baton’s school.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Such is that regard to character which is so strong in those who have been accustomed to introduce it of themselves and conjoined with other things into their deliberations.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: How, he replied, does the bull alone, when the lion has attacked, discover his own powers and put himself forward in defense of the whole herd?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is plain that with the powers the perception of having them is immediately conjoined: and, therefore, whoever of us has such powers will not be ignorant of them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now a bull is not made suddenly, nor a brave man; but we must discipline ourselves in the winter for the summer campaign, and not rashly run upon that which does not concern us.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Of all the faculties (except that which I shall soon mention), you will find not one which is capable of contemplating itself, and, consequently, not capable either of approving or disapproving.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The rational faculty; for this is the only faculty that we have received which examines itself, what it is, and what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all other faculties: for what else is there which tells us that golden things are beautiful, for they do not say so themselves?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What else judges of music, grammar, and the other faculties, proves their uses, and points out the occasions for using them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But when you must write something to your friend, grammar will tell you what words you should write; but whether you should write or not, grammar will not tell you.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And so it is with music as to musical sounds; but whether you should sing at the present time and play on the lute, or do neither, music will not tell you.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Only consider at what price you sell your own will: if for no other reason, at least for this, that you sell it not for a small sum.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Epictetus is not superior to Socrates; but if he is not inferior, this is enough for me; for I shall never be a Milo, and yet I do not neglect my body; nor shall I be a Croesus, and yet I do not neglect my property; nor, in a word, do we neglect looking after anything because we despair of reaching the highest degree.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If a man should be able to assent to this doctrine as he ought, that we are all sprung from God in an especial manner, and that God is the father both of men and of gods, I suppose that he would never have any ignoble or mean thoughts about himself.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if Caesar (the emperor) should adopt you, no one could endure your arrogance; and if you know that you are the son of Zeus, will you not be elated?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Yet we do not so; but since these two things are mingled in the generation of man, body in common with the animals, and reason and intelligence in common with the gods, many incline to this kinship which is miserable and mortal; and some few to that which is divine and happy.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Since then it is of necessity that every man uses everything according to the opinion which he has about it, those, the few, who think that they are formed for fidelity and modesty and a sure use of appearances have no mean or ignoble thoughts about themselves; but with the many it is quite the contrary.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Through this kinship with the flesh, some of us inclining to it become like wolves, faithless and treacherous and mischievous; some become like lions, savage and bestial and untamed; but the greater part of us become foxes, and other worse animals.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For what else is a slanderer and a malignant man than a fox, or some other more wretched and meaner animal?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: He who is making progress, having learned from philosophers that desire means the desire of good things, and aversion means aversion from bad things; having learned too that happiness and tranquillity are not attainable by man otherwise than by not failing to obtain what he desires, and not falling into that which he would avoid; such a man takes from himself desire altogether and defers it, but he employs his aversion only on things which are dependent on his will.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For if he attempts to avoid anything independent of his will, he knows that sometimes he will fall in with something which he wishes to avoid, and he will be unhappy.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now if virtue promises good fortune and tranquillity and happiness, certainly also the progress towards virtue is progress towards each of these things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For it is always true that to whatever point the perfecting of anything leads us, progress is an approach towards this point.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: How then do we admit that virtue is such as I have said, and yet seek progress in other things and make a display of it?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In desire and in aversion, that you may not be disappointed in your desire, and that you may not fall into that which you would avoid; in your pursuit and avoiding, that you commit no error; in assent and suspension of assent, that you be not deceived.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if with trembling and lamentation you seek not to fall into that which you avoid, tell me how you are improving.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But now we admit that virtue produces one thing, and we declare that approaching near to it is another thing: namely, progress or improvement.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If I were talking to an athlete, I should say: Show me your shoulders; and then he might say, “Here are my Halteres.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I reply, “Slave, I am not inquiring about this, but how you exercise pursuit and avoidance, desire and aversion, how you design and purpose and prepare yourself, whether conformably to nature or not.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If conformably, give me evidence of it, and I will say that you are making progress: but if not conformably, be gone, and not only expound your books, but write such books yourself; and what will you gain by it?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For what else is tragedy than the perturbations (πάθη) of men who value externals exhibited in this kind of poetry?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if a man must learn by fiction that no external things which are independent of the will concern us, for my part I should like this fiction, by the aid of which I should live happily and undisturbed.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if he has strained his efforts to the practice of reading books, and labors only at this, and has travelled for this, I tell him to return home immediately, and not to neglect his affairs there; for this for which he has travelled is nothing.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But the other thing is something, to study how a man can rid his life of lamentation and groaning, and saying, “Woe to me, and wretched that I am,” and to rid it also of misfortune and disappointment, and to learn what death is, and exile, and prison, and poison, that he may be able to say when he is in fetters, “Dear Crito, if it is the will of the gods that it be so, let it be so;” and not to say, “Wretched am I, an old man; have I kept my grey hairs for this?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The reply is, to know that these things are not false, from which happiness comes and tranquillity arises.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Take my books, and you will learn how true and conformable to nature are the things which make me free from perturbations.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: To Triptolemus all men have erected temples and altars, because he gave us food by cultivation; but to him who discovered truth and brought it to light and communicated it to all, not the truth which shows us how to live, but how to live well, who of you for this reason has built an altar, or a temple, or has dedicated a statue, or who worships God for this?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Because the gods have given the vine, or wheat, we sacrifice to them: but because they have produced in the human mind that fruit by which they designed to show us the truth which relates to happiness, shall we not thank God for this?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As then it was fit to be so, that which is best of all and supreme over all is the only thing which the gods have placed in our power, the right use of appearances; but all other things they have not placed in our power.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I indeed think that, if they had been able, they would have put these other things also in our power, but they certainly could not.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For as we exist on the earth, and are bound to such a body and to such companions, how was it possible for us not to be hindered as to these things by externals?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If a man, said Epictetus, opposes evident truths, it is not easy to find arguments by which we shall make him change his opinion.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But this does not arise either from the man’s strength or the teacher’s weakness; for when the man, though he has been confuted, is hardened like a stone, how shall we then be able to deal with him by argument?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now there are two kinds of hardening, one of the understanding, the other of the sense of shame, when a man is resolved not to assent to what is manifest nor to desist from contradictions.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Most of us are afraid of mortification of the body, and would contrive all means to avoid such a thing, but we care not about the soul’s mortification.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And indeed with regard to the soul, if a man be in such a state as not to apprehend anything, or understand at all, we think that he is in a bad condition: but if the sense of shame and modesty are deadened, this we call even power (or strength).
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Another does see it, but he is not moved, and makes no improvement: he is even in a worse condition.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: His modesty is extirpated, and his sense of shame; and the rational faculty has not been cut off from him, but it is brutalised.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Certainly not, unless we also name it such in catamites, through which they do and say in public whatever comes into their head.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: From everything which is or happens in the world, it is easy to praise Providence, if a man possesses these two qualities, the faculty of seeing what belongs and happens to all persons and things, and a grateful disposition.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And, indeed, from the very structure of things which have attained their completion, we are accustomed to show that the work is certainly the act of some artificer, and that it has not been constructed without a purpose.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Does then each of these things demonstrate the workman, and do not visible things and the faculty of seeing and light demonstrate Him?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And the existence of male and female, and the desire of each for conjunction, and the power of using the parts which are constructed, do not even these declare the workman?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If they do not, let us consider the constitution of our understanding according to which, when we meet with sensible objects, we do not simply receive impressions from them, but we also select something from them, and subtract something, and add, and compound by means of them these things or those, and, in fact, pass from some to other things which, in a manner, resemble them: is not even this sufficient to move some men, and to induce them not to forget the workman?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If not so, let them explain to us what it is that makes each several thing, or how it is possible that things so wonderful and like the contrivances of art should exist by chance and from their own proper motion?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If he does not possess these two qualities, one man will not see the use of things which are and which happen; another will not be thankful for them, even if he does know them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If God had made colors, but had not made the faculty of seeing them, what would have been their use?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: On the other hand, if He had made the faculty of vision, but had not made objects such as to fall under the faculty, what in that case also would have been the use of it?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Well then God constitutes every animal: one to be eaten, another to serve for agriculture, another to supply cheese, and another for some like use; for which purposes what need is there to understand appearances and to be able to distinguish them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But God has introduced man to be a spectator of God and of His works; and not only a spectator of them, but an interpreter.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For this reason it is shameful for man to begin and to end where irrational animals do; but rather he ought to begin where they begin, and to end where nature ends in us; and nature ends in contemplation and understanding, and in a way of life conformable to nature.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Many, indeed, in us only, of which the rational animal had peculiarly need; but you will find many common to us with irrational animals.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For use is one thing, and understanding is another: God had need of irrational animals to make use of appearances, but of us to understand the use of appearances.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is therefore enough for them to eat and to drink, and to sleep and to copulate, and to do all the other things which they severally do.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But for us, to whom He has given also the intellectual faculty, these things are not sufficient; for unless we act in a proper and orderly manner, and conformably to the nature and constitution of each thing, we shall never attain our true end.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For where the constitutions of living beings are different, there also the acts and the ends are different.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In those animals then whose constitution is adapted only to use, use alone is enough; but in an animal (man), which has also the power of understanding the use, unless there be the due exercise of the understanding he will never attain his proper end.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But you take a journey to Olympia to see the work of Phidias, and all of you think it a misfortune to die without having seen such things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But I suppose that setting all these things off against the magnificence of the spectacle, you bear and endure.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Shall I not use the power for the purposes for which I received it, and shall I grieve and lament over what happens?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But when there is no need to take a journey, and where a man is, there he has the works (of God) before him, will you not desire to see and understand them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Will you not perceive either what you are, or what you were born for, or what this is for which you have received the faculty of sight?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and what the use of his arms, and of the strength of the other parts of his body, and his endurance and noble spirit, if such circumstances and occasions had not roused and exercised him?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Well then must a man provide for himself such means of exercise, and seek to introduce a lion from some place into his country, and a boar, and a hydra?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: This would be folly and madness: but as they did exist, and were found, they were useful for showing what Hercules was and for exercising him.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Come then do you also, having observed these things, look to the faculties which you have, and when you have looked at them, say: Bring now, O Zeus, any difficulty that thou pleasest, for I have means given to me by thee and powers for honoring myself through the things which happen.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You do not so: but you sit still, trembling for fear that some things will happen, and weeping, and lamenting, and groaning for what does happen; and then you blame the gods.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And yet God has not only given us these faculties by which we shall be able to bear everything thing happens without being depressed or broken by it, but, like a good king and a true father, He has given us these faculties free from hindrance, subject to no compulsion, unimpeded, and has put them entirely in our own power, without even having reserved to Himself any power of hindering or impeding.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You, who have received these powers free and as your own, use them not: you do not even see what you have received, and from whom; some of you being blinded to the giver, and not even acknowledging your benefactor, and others, through meanness of spirit, betaking yourselves to faultfinding and making charges against God.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Yet I will show to you that you have powers and means for greatness of soul and manliness: but what powers you have for finding fault and making accusations, do you show me.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What do you think that Hercules would have been if there had not been such a lion, and hydra, and stag, and boar, and certain unjust and bestial men, whom Hercules used to drive away and clear out?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In the first place then he would not have been a Hercules, when he was dreaming away all his life in such luxury and ease; and even if he had been one, what would have been the use of him?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And will you be vexed and discontented with the things established by Zeus, which he with the Moirae (fates) who were present and spinning the thread of your generation, defined and put in order?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I mean with respect to the body, for as to intelligence you are not inferior to the gods nor less; for the magnitude of intelligence is not measured by length nor yet by height, but by thoughts.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you not rather thank the gods that they have allowed you to be above these things which they have not placed in your power, and have made you accountable only for those which are in your power?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As to your parents, the gods have left you free from responsibility; and so with respect to your brothers, and your body, and possessions, and death and life.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What then, was it permitted to you to come forth and to select and to say: Let such a man at this moment unite with such a woman that I may be produced?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It was not permitted, but it was a necessity for your parents to exist first, and then for you to be begotten.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now if you did not know for what purpose you possess the faculty of vision, you would be unfortunate and wretched if you closed your eyes when colors were brought before them; but in that you possess greatness of soul and nobility of spirit for every event that may happen, and you know not that you possess them, are you not more unfortunate and wretched?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Things are brought close to you which are proportionate to the power which you possess, but you turn away this power most particularly at the very time when you ought to maintain it open and discerning.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: These are the things which philosophers should meditate on, which they should write daily, in which they should exercise themselves.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When someone asked how may a man eat acceptably to the gods, he answered: If he can eat justly and contentedly, and with equanimity, and temperately and orderly, will it not be also acceptably to the gods?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But when you have asked for warm water and the slave has not heard, or if he did hear has brought only tepid water, or he is not even found to be in the house, then not to be vexed or to burst with passion, is not this acceptable to the gods?

quotes.text: Slave yourself, will you not bear with your own brother, who has Zeus for his progenitor, and is like a son from the same seeds and of the same descent from above?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you see in what direction you are looking, that it is towards the earth, towards the pit, that it is towards these wretched laws of dead men?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When a person asked him how a man could be convinced that all his actions are under the inspection of God, he answered: Do you not think that all things are united in one?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and when He bids them to fold themselves up and to remain quiet and rest, how else do they remain quiet and rest?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And how else at the growth and the wane of the moon, and at the approach and recession of the sun, are so great an alteration and change to the contrary seen in earthly things?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But are plants and our bodies so bound up and united with the whole, and are not our souls much more?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and our souls so bound up and in contact with God as parts of Him and portions of Him; and does not God perceive every motion of these parts as being his own motion connate with himself?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now are you able to think of the divine administration, and about all things divine, and at the same time also about human affairs, and to be moved by ten thousand things at the same time in your senses and in your understanding, and to assent to some, and to dissent from others, and again as to some things to suspend your judgment; and do you retain in your soul so many impressions from so many and various things, and being moved by them, do you fall upon notions similar to those first impressed, and do you retain numerous arts and the memories of ten thousand things; and is not God able to oversee all things, and to be present with all, and to receive from all a certain communication?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And is the sun able to illuminate so large a part of the All, and to leave so little not illuminated, that part only which is occupied by the earth’s shadow; and He who made the sun itself and makes it go round, being a small part of himself compared with the whole, cannot He perceive all things?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And how else so regularly as if by God’s command, when He bids the plants to flower, do they flower?

quotes.text: Do not wonder if for other animals than man all things are provided for the body, not only food and drink, but beds also, and they have no need of shoes nor bed materials, nor clothing; but we require all these additional things.

quotes.text: For animals not being made for themselves, but for service, it was not fit for them to be made so as to need other things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For consider what it would be for us to take care not only of ourselves, but also about cattle and asses, how they should be clothed, and how shod, and how they should eat and drink.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now as soldiers are ready for their commander, shod, clothed, and armed: but it would be a hard thing for the chiliarch (tribune) to go round and shoe or clothe his thousand men: so also nature has formed the animals which are made for service, all ready, prepared, and requiring no further care.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But now we, instead of being thankful that we need not take the same care of animals as of ourselves, complain of God on our own account; and yet, in the name of Zeus and the gods, any one thing of those which exist would be enough to make a man perceive the providence of God, at least a man who is modest and grateful.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And speak not to me now of the great things, but only of this, that milk is produced from grass, and cheese from milk, and wool from skins.

quotes.text: For if we had understanding, ought we to do anything else both jointly and severally than to sing hymns and bless the deity, and to tell of his benefits?

quotes.text: “Great is God, who has given us such implements with which we shall cultivate the earth: great is God who has given us hands, the power of swallowing, a stomach, imperceptible growth, and the power of breathing while we sleep.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: This is what we ought to sing on every occasion, and to sing the greatest and most divine hymn for giving us the faculty of comprehending these things and using a proper way.

quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Nor do we need a diviner (sacrificer) on his own account, but because we think that through him we shall know the future and understand the signs given by the gods; nor do we need the viscera of animals for their own sake, but because through them signs are given; nor do we look with wonder on the crow or raven, but on God, who through them gives signs?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —As to this indeed we shall see: but then even if a man should grant this, it is enough that logic has the power of distinguishing and examining other things, and, as we may say, of measuring and weighing them.

quotes.text: I go then to the interpreter of these things and the sacrificer, and I say: Inspect the viscera for me, and tell me what signs they give.

quotes.text: No; it is not what is placed before you that compels, but your opinion that it is better to do so-and-so than to die.

quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For the sake of this divination I go to this diviner and to the philosopher, not admiring him for this interpretation, but admiring the things which he interprets.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The man takes the viscera, opens them, and interprets: Man, he says, you have a will free by nature from hindrance and compulsion; this is written here in the viscera.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You see that in this matter you have the faculty of the will free from hindrance, free from compulsion, unimpeded.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If what philosophers say is true, that all men have one principle, as in the case of assent the persuasion that a thing is so, and in the case of dissent the persuasion that a thing is not so, and in the case of a suspense of judgment the persuasion that a thing is uncertain, so also in the case of a movement towards any thing the persuasion that a thing is for a man’s advantage, and it is impossible to think that one thing is advantageous and to desire another, and to judge one thing to be proper and to move towards another, why then are we angry with the many?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When it was reported to him that his trial was going on in the Senate, he said, “I hope it may turn out well; but it is the fifth hour of the day”—this was the time when he was used to exercise himself and then take the cold bath—“let us go and take our exercise.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Learn that a thief and an adulterer have no place in the things which are yours, but in those which belong to others and which are not in your power.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But so long as you value these things, be angry with yourself rather than with the thief and the adulterer.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Consider the matter thus: you have fine clothes; your neighbour has not: you have a window; you wish to air the clothes.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The thief does not know wherein man’s good consists, but he thinks that it consists in having fine clothes, the very thing which you also think.

quotes.text: For the future, relying on these opinions, walk about upright, free; not trusting to the size of your body, as an athlete, for a man ought not to be invincible in the way that an ass is.

quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: This is not a perverse self-regard, for the animal is constituted so as to do all things for itself.

quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The propositions which are true and evident are of necessity used even by those who contradict them: and a man might perhaps consider it to be the greatest proof of a thing being evident that it is found to be necessary even for him who denies it to make use of it at the same time.

quotes.text: For instance, if a man should deny that there is anything universally true, it is plain that he must make the contradictory negation, that nothing is universally true.

quotes.text: Again if a man should come forward and say: “Know that there is nothing that can be known, but all things are incapable of sure evidence;” or if another say, “Believe me and you will be the better for it, that a man ought not to believe anything;” or again, if another should say, “Learn from me, man, that it is not possible to learn anything; I tell you this and will teach you, if you choose.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Thus Epicurus also, when he designs to destroy the natural fellowship of mankind, at the same time makes use of that which he destroys.

quotes.text: For if this is so, lie down and sleep, and lead the life of a worm, of which you judged yourself worthy: eat and drink, and enjoy women, and ease yourself, and snore.

quotes.text: Would it not be a desirable thing if men could be lulled and enchanted by the Stoics, and sleep and present themselves to you and to those like you to be shorn and milked?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For this you ought to say to your brother Epicureans: but ought you not to conceal it from others, and particularly before everything to persuade them, that we are by nature adapted for fellowship, that temperance is a good thing; in order that all things may be secured for you?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: “Be not deceived, men, nor be led astray, nor be mistaken: there is no natural fellowship among rational animals; believe me.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What then was it that waked Epicurus from his sleepiness, and compelled him to write what he did write?

quotes.text: What a shame is this: when a man has received from nature measures and rules for the knowing of truth, and does not strive to add to these measures and rules and to improve them, but just the contrary, endeavors to take away and destroy whatever enables us to discern the truth?

quotes.text: What else was it than that which is the strongest thing in men: nature, which draws a man to her own will though he be unwilling and complaining?

quotes.text: For since, she says, you think that there is no community among mankind, write this opinion and leave it for others, and break your sleep to do this, and by your own practice condemn your own opinions.

quotes.text: Shall we then say that Orestes was agitated by the Erinyes (Furies) and roused from his deep sleep, and did not more savage Erinyes and Pains rouse Epicurus from his sleep and not allow him to rest, but compelled him to make known his own evils, as madness and wine did the Galli (the priests of Cybele)?

quotes.text: So strong and invincible is man’s nature: For how can a vine be moved not in the manner of a vine, but in the manner of an olive tree?

quotes.text: Well done, philosopher, you have done something for our citizens, you have brought back all the young men to contempt of things divine.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: An appearance was presented to me, I swear by your genius, which could not be distinguished from oil and was exactly like it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —If I had three or four fellow-slaves of the same opinion, I should force him to hang himself through passion or to change his mind.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If he said, “Boy, throw some olive oil into the bath,” I would take pickle sauce and pour it down on his head.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Grateful indeed are men and modest, who, if they do nothing else, are daily eating bread and yet are shameless enough to say, we do not know if there is a Demeter or her daughter Persephone or a Pluto; not to mention that they are enjoying the night and the day, the seasons of the year, and the stars, and the sea and the land and the cooperation of mankind, and yet they are not moved in any degree by these things to turn their attention to them; but they only seek to belch out their little problem (matter for discussion), and when they have exercised their stomach to go off to the bath.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But what they shall say, and about what things or to what persons, and what their hearers shall learn from this talk, they care not even in the least degree, nor do they care if any generous youth after hearing such talk should suffer any harm from it, nor after he has suffered harm should lose all the seeds of his generous nature; nor if we should give an adulterer help towards being shameless in his acts; nor if a public peculator should lay hold of some cunning excuse from these doctrines; nor if another who neglects his parents should be confirmed in his audacity by this teaching.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —Why then should a man say any more in reply to such persons as these, or give them any reason or listen to any reason from them, or try to convince them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: By Zeus one might much sooner expect to make catamites change their mind than those who are become so deaf and blind to their own evils.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: The judge will determine against you something that appears formidable; but that you should also suffer in trying to avoid it, how can he do that?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When then the pursuit of objects and the avoiding of them are in your power, what else do you care for?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Let this be your preface, this your narrative, this your confirmation, this your victory, this your peroration, this your applause (or the approbation which you will receive).
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For if you wish to maintain a will conformable to nature, you have every security, every facility, you have no troubles.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For if you wish to maintain what is in your own power and is naturally free, and if you are content with these, what else do you care for?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you choose not to be restrained or compelled, who shall compel you to desire what you think that you ought not to desire?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But they suppose timidity to be a characteristic of a good disposition, and compassion also; but silliness to be the absolute characteristic of a slave.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But in the case of most errors for this reason chiefly they are induced to confess them, because they imagine that there is something involuntary in them as in timidity and compassion; and if a man confess that he is in any respect intemperate, he alleges love (or passion) as an excuse for what is involuntary.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: There is also in jealousy, as they suppose, something involuntary; and for this reason they confess to jealousy also.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, “I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But men readily confess that they are timid, and they say: “I am rather timid, I confess; but as to other respects you will not find me to be foolish.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: A man will not readily confess that he is intemperate; and that he is unjust, he will not confess at all.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —The chief thing (the ruling thing) is inconsistency and confusion in the things which relate to good and evil.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But different men have different reasons; and generally what they imagine to be base, they do not confess at all.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Living then among such men, who are so confused, so ignorant of what they say, and of the evils which they have or have not, and why they have them, or how they shall be relieved of them, I think it is worth the trouble for a man to watch constantly (and to ask) whether I also am one of them, what imagination I have about myself, how I conduct myself, whether I conduct myself as a prudent man, whether I conduct myself as a temperate man, whether I ever say this: that I have been taught to be prepared for everything that may happen.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: or do I like a snivelling boy go to my school to learn history and understand the books which I did not understand before, and, if it should happen so, to explain them also to others?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: —Man, you have had a fight in the house with a poor slave, you have turned the family upside down, you have frightened the neighbours, and you come to me as if you were a wise man, and you take your seat and judge how I have explained some word, and how I have babbled whatever came into my head.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You come full of envy, and humbled, because you bring nothing from home; and you sit during the discussion thinking of nothing else than how your father is disposed towards you and your brother.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I wish I could learn everything before I return: but much labor is necessary, and no one sends me anything, and the baths at Nicopolis are dirty; everything is bad at home, and bad here.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: “Yes; but if my child die or my brother, or if I must die or be racked, what good will these things do me?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: or, when you went out to the walking place, did you ever propose any appearance that had been presented to you instead of a syllogism, and did you and your friends discuss it together?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you ask me now if syllogisms are useful, I will tell you that they are useful, and if you choose, I will prove it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And do you, O men, first cure the ulcers and stop the discharge; be tranquil in your mind, bring it free from distraction into the school, and you will know what power reason has.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For you come not to lay aside (your principles) or to correct them or to receive other principles in place of them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It remains then that they employ themselves earnestly only about things which are good; and if they are earnestly employed about things, they love such things also.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Whoever then understands what is good, can also know how to love: but he who cannot distinguish good from bad, and things which are neither good nor bad from both, how can he possess the power of loving?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But wealth, and pleasure, and in a word things themselves, do you sometimes think them to be good, and sometimes bad?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and have you not at one time a friendly feeling towards them, and at another time the feeling of an enemy?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And he who has selected a man as his friend and is of a changeable disposition, has he good will towards him?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Well then, did you never see little dogs caressing and playing with one another, so that you might say, there is nothing more friendly?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Throw between yourself and your son a little estate, and you will know how soon he will wish to bury you and how soon you wish your son to die.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Throw a smart girl between you; and do you the old man love her, and the young one will love her too.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is in truth because you are often disturbed by appearances and perplexed, and their power of persuasion often conquers you; and sometimes you think these things to be good, and then the same things to be bad, and lastly neither good nor bad; and in short you grieve, fear, envy, are disturbed, you are changed.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Were they not brought up together; had they not lived together, drunk together, slept together, and often kissed one another?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: So that if any man, I think, had seen them, he would have ridiculed the philosophers for the paradoxes which they utter about friendship.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For universally, be not deceived, every animal is attached to nothing so much as to its own interest.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Whatever then appears to it an impediment to this interest, whether this be a brother, or a father, or a child, or beloved, or lover, it hates, spurns, curses: for its nature is to love nothing so much as its own interest; this is father, and brother and kinsman, and country, and God.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When then the gods appear to us to be an impediment to this, we abuse them and throw down their statues and burn their temples, as Alexander ordered the temples of Aesculapius to be burned when his dear friend died.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Therefore Socrates said to one who was reminding him to prepare for his trial, “Do you not think then that I have been preparing for it all my life?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For this reason if a man put in the same place his interest, sanctity, goodness, and country, and parents, and friends, all these are secured: but if he puts in one place his interest, in another his friends, and his country and his kinsmen and justice itself, all these give way being borne down by the weight of interest.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For where the I and the Mine are placed, to that place of necessity the animal inclines: if in the flesh, there is the ruling power: if in the will, it is there: and if it is in externals, it is there.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If then I am there where my will is, then only shall I be a friend such as I ought to be, and son, and father; for this will be my interest, to maintain the character of fidelity, of modesty, of patience, of abstinence, of active cooperation, of observing my relations (towards all).
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if I put myself in one place, and honesty in another, then the doctrine of Epicurus becomes strong, which asserts either that there is no honesty or it is that which opinion holds to be honest (virtuous).
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It was through this ignorance that the Athenians and the Lacedaemonians quarrelled, and the Thebans with both; and the great king quarrelled with Hellas, and the Macedonians with both; and the Romans with the Getae.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if you hear that in truth these men think the good to be only there, where will is, and where there is a right use of appearances, no longer trouble yourself whether they are father or son, or brothers, or have associated a long time and are companions, but when you have ascertained this only, confidently declare that they are friends, as you declare that they are faithful, that they are just.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For where else is friendship than where there is fidelity, and modesty, where there is a communion of honest things and of nothing else?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Alexander was the guest of Menelaus; and if any man had seen their friendly disposition, he would not have believed anyone who said that they were not friends.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But there was cast between them (as between dogs) a bit of meat, a handsome woman, and about her war arose.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And now when you see brothers to be friends appearing to have one mind, do not conclude from this anything about their friendship, not even if they swear it and say that it is impossible for them to be separated from one another.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For the ruling principle of a bad man cannot be trusted; it is insecure, has no certain rule by which it is directed, and is overpowered at different times by different appearances.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But examine, not what other men examine—if they are born of the same parents and brought up together, and under the same pedagogue—but examine this only, wherein they place their interest, whether in externals or in the will.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If in externals, do not name them friends, no more than name them trustworthy or constant, or brave or free: do not name them even men, if you have any judgment.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For that is not a principle of human nature which makes them bite one another, and abuse one another, and occupy deserted places or public places, as if they were mountains, and in the courts of justice display the acts of robbers; nor yet that which makes them intemperate and adulterers and corrupters, nor that which makes them do whatever else men do against one another through this one opinion only, that of placing themselves and their interests in the things which are not within the power of their will.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And thus first of all he will not reproach himself, he will not be at variance with himself, he will not change his mind, he will not torture himself.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In the next place, to another also, who is like himself, he will be altogether and completely a friend.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But he will bear with the man who is unlike himself, he will be kind to him, gentle, ready to pardon on account of his ignorance, on account of his being mistaken in things of the greatest importance; but he will be harsh to no man, being well convinced of Plato’s doctrine that every mind is deprived of truth unwillingly.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If you cannot do this, yet you can do in all other respects as friends do—drink together, and lodge together, and sail together—and you may be born of the same parents—for snakes also are—but neither will they be friends nor you, so long as you retain these bestial and cursed opinions.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: How do you know, slave, if he did not regard you in the same way as he wipes his shoes with a sponge, or as he takes care of his beast?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: How do you know, when you have ceased to be useful as a vessel, he will not throw you away like a broken platter?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: That was the bestial principle, that was the thing which broke asunder the friendship between husband and wife, that which did not allow the woman to be a wife nor the mother to be a mother.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And let every man among you who has seriously resolved either to be a friend himself or to have another for his friend, cut out these opinions, hate them, drive them from his soul.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Every man will read a book with more pleasure, or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Therefore every man will also listen more readily to what is spoken, if it is signified by appropriate and becoming words.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: We must not say then that there is no faculty of expression: for this affirmation is the characteristic of an impious and also of a timid man.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Of an impious man, because he undervalues the gifts which come from God, just as if he would take away the commodity of the power of vision, or of hearing, or of seeing.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and to no purpose has he infused into them a spirit so strong and of such skillful contrivance as to reach a long way and to fashion the forms of things which are seen?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And to no purpose has he made the interjacent atmosphere so efficacious and elastic that the vision penetrates through the atmosphere which is in a manner moved?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And to no purpose has he made light, without the presence of which there would be no use in any other thing?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: How then can any other faculty be more powerful than this, which uses the rest as ministers and itself proves each and pronounces about them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: what faculty is it which opens and closes the eyes, and turns them away from objects to which it ought not to apply them and does apply them to other objects?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But indeed for the power of seeing and hearing, and indeed for life itself, and for the things which contribute to support it, for the fruits which are dry, and for wine and oil give thanks to God.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Will this faculty then, seeing that it is amidst all the other faculties which are blind and dumb and unable to see anything else except the very acts for which they are appointed in order to minister to this (faculty) and serve it, but this faculty alone sees sharp and sees what is the value of each of the rest; will this faculty declare to us that anything else is the best, or that itself is?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And whether we ought to believe what is said or not to believe it, and if we do believe, whether we ought to be moved by it or not, who tells us?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But this faculty of speaking and of ornamenting words, if there is indeed any such peculiar faculty, what else does it do, when there happens to be discourse about a thing, than to ornament the words and arrange them as hairdressers do the hair?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But whether it is better to speak or to be silent, and better to speak in this way or that way, and whether this is becoming or not becoming, and the season for each and the use, what else tells us than the faculty of the will?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But remember that he has given you something else better than all these: I mean the power of using them, proving them and estimating the value of each.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No; but they are appointed as ministers and slaves to serve the faculty which has the power of making use of the appearances of things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and how is it possible that the things which are subject to restraint are stronger than that which is not?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: it (the will) says, if the fact is so, can that which ministers be superior to that to which it ministers, can the horse be superior to the rider, or the dog to the huntsman, or the instrument to the musician, or the servants to the king?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: What destroys the whole man, at one time by hunger, at another time by hanging, and at another time by a precipice?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then being so great a faculty and set over all the rest, let it (the will) come forward and tell us that the most excellent of all things is the flesh.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Not even if the flesh itself declared that it is the most excellent, would any person bear that it should say this.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But what is it, Epicurus, which pronounces this, which wrote about the End (purpose) of our Being, which wrote on the Nature of Things, which wrote about the Canon (rule of truth), which led you to wear a beard, which wrote when it was dying that it was spending the last and a happy day?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When then I speak thus, let no man think that I ask you to neglect the power of speaking, for neither do I ask you to neglect the eyes, nor the ears nor the hands nor the feet, nor clothing nor shoes.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For it is this which uses the other (the power of speaking), and all the other faculties both small and great.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For when this faculty of the will is set right, a man who is not good becomes good: but when it fails, a man becomes bad.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is through this that we are unfortunate, that we are fortunate, that we blame one another, are pleased with one another.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In a word, it is this which if we neglect it makes unhappiness, and if we carefully look after it, makes happiness.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For there is some use even in an ass, but not so much as in an ox: there is also use in a dog, but not so much as in a slave: there is also some use in a slave, but not so much as in citizens: there is also some use in citizens, but not so much as in magistrates.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But to take away the faculty of speaking and to say that there is no such faculty in reality, is the act not only of an ungrateful man towards those who gave it, but also of a cowardly man: for such a person seems to me to fear, if there is any faculty of this kind, that we shall not be able to despise it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then it would happen that a man would be affected in the same way if he saw Thersites and if he saw Achilles; in the same way, if he saw Helen and any other woman.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But these are foolish and clownish notions, and the notions of men who know not the nature of each thing, but are afraid, if a man shall see the difference, that he shall immediately be seized and carried off vanquished.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But this is the great matter; to leave to each thing the power (faculty) which it has, and leaving to it this power to see what is the worth of the power, and to learn what is the most excellent of all things, and to pursue this always, to be diligent about this, considering all other things of secondary value compared with this, but yet, as far as we can, not neglecting all those other things.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For we must take care of the eyes also, not as if they were the most excellent thing, but we must take care of them on account of the most excellent thing, because it will not be in its true natural condition, if it does not rightly use the other faculties, and prefer some things to others.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But if you wish to maintain externals also—your poor body, your little property and your little estimation—I advise you to make from this moment all possible preparation, and then consider both the nature of your judge and your adversary.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For when you have subjected to externals what is your own, then be a slave and do not resist, and do not sometimes choose to be a slave, and sometimes not choose, but with all your mind be one or the other, either free or a slave, either instructed or uninstructed, either a well bred cock or a mean one, either endure to be beaten until you die or yield at once; and let it not happen to you to receive many stripes and then to yield.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: It is where truth is: where truth is and where nature is, there is caution: where truth is, there is courage where nature is.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Since by the aid of speech and such communication as you receive here you must advance to perfection, and purge your will and correct the faculty which makes use of the appearances of things; and since it is necessary also for the teaching (delivery) of theorems to be effected by a certain mode of expression and with a certain variety and sharpness, some persons captivated by these very things abide in them, one captivated by the expression, another by syllogisms, another again by sophisms, and still another by some other inn (πανδοκείου) of the kind; and there they stay and waste away as if they were among Sirens.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Men generally act as a traveller would do on his way to his own country, when he enters a good inn, and being pleased with it should remain there.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Man, you have forgotten your purpose: you were not travelling to this inn, but you were passing through it.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But your purpose is this, to return to your country, to relieve your kinsmen of anxiety, to discharge the duties of a citizen, to marry, to beget children, to fill the usual magistracies.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For you are not come to select more pleasant places, but to live in these where you were born and of which you were made a citizen.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then having this purpose before you, if some little form of expression pleases you, if some theorems please you, do you abide among them and choose to dwell there, forgetting the things at home, and do you say, “These things are fine?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: If a man by this teaching does harm to those who listen to him, reckon me too among those who do this harm: for I am not able, when I see one thing which is most excellent and supreme, to say that another is so, in order to please you.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and what prevents you, if you can resolve syllogisms like Chrysippus, from being wretched, from sorrowing, from envying, in a word, from being disturbed, from being unhappy?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: You see then that these were inns, worth nothing; and that the purpose before you was something else.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When I speak thus to some persons, they think that I am rejecting care about speaking or care about theorems.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But I am not rejecting this care, but I am rejecting the abiding about these things incessantly and putting our hopes in them.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: A certain person said to him (Epictetus): “Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer: and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me.”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you think, said Epictetus, that as there is an art in anything else, so there is also an art in speaking, and that he who has the art, will speak skillfully, and he who has not, will speak unskillfully?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Then if speaking properly is the business of the skillful man, do you see that to hear also with benefit is the business of the skillful man?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Now as to speaking and hearing perfectly, and usefully, let us for the present, if you please, say no more, for both of us are a long way from everything of the kind.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But I think that every man will allow this: that he who is going to hear philosophers requires some amount of practice in hearing.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: He then who by speaking receives benefit himself, and is able to benefit others, will speak skillfully: but he who is rather damaged by speaking and does damage to others, will he be unskilled in this art of speaking?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: In this case also then those who hear skillfully are benefited, and those who hear unskillfully are damaged?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you understand this very thing, what demonstration is, or how anything is demonstrated, or by what means; or what things are like demonstration, but are not demonstration?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Shall I show to you the repugnance in the opinions of most men, through which they differ about things good and evil, and about things which are profitable and unprofitable, when you know not this very thing, what repugnance (contradiction) is?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: As the grass which is suitable, when it is presented to a sheep, moves its inclination to eat, but if you present to it a stone or bread, it will not be moved to eat; so there are in us certain natural inclinations also to speak, when the hearer shall appear to be somebody, when he himself shall excite us: but when he shall sit by us like a stone or like grass, how can he excite a man’s desire (to speak)?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: No, but the vine by showing in itself that it will be profitable to the husbandman, if he does take care of it, invites him to exercise care.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When children are attractive and lively, whom do they not invite to play with them, and crawl with them, and lisp with them?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do we know then what a man is, what the notion is which we have of him, or have we our ears in any degree practiced about this matter?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And do you, most excellent Sir, neglect the duties of the king, you who are the people’s guardian and have such cares?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and are you quarrelling about a little girl with the most warlike of your allies, whom you ought by every means to take care of and protect?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: and do you become worse than (inferior to) a well behaved priest who treats you these fine gladiators with all respect?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: I can only say this to you, that he who knows not who he is, and for what purpose he exists, and what is this world, and with whom he is associated, and what things are the good and the bad, and the beautiful and the ugly, and who neither understands discourse nor demonstration, nor what is true nor what is false, and who is not able to distinguish them, will neither desire according to nature nor turn away nor move towards, nor intend (to act), nor assent nor dissent, nor suspend his judgment: to say all in a few words, he will go about dumb and blind, thinking that he is somebody, but being nobody.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Is it not the fact that ever since the human race existed, all errors and misfortunes have arisen through this ignorance?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Does not the one say it is profitable to restore Chryseis to her father, and does not the other say that it is not profitable?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Does not the one say that he ought to take the prize of another, and does not the other say that he ought not?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When you would listen to a philosopher, do not say to him, “You tell me nothing;” but only show yourself worthy of hearing or fit for hearing; and you will see how you will move the speaker.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For what must I look to in order to be roused, as men who are expert in riding are roused by generous horses?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For if you wish to be crucified, wait and the cross will come: but if you choose to submit and to plead your cause as well as you can, you must do what is consistent with this object, provided you maintain what is your own (your proper character).
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: do you think that, if Socrates had wished to preserve externals, he would have come forward and said: “Anytus and Melitus can certainly kill me, but to harm me they are not able?”
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Was he so foolish as not to see that this way leads not to the preservation of life and fortune, but to another end?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Just in the same way my friend Heraclitus, who had a little suit in Rhodes about a bit of land, and had proved to the judges (δικασταῖς) that his case was just, said when he had come to the peroration of his speech, I will neither entreat you nor do I care what judgment you will give, and it is you rather than I who are on your trial.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Only do not entreat; but do not also say “I do not entreat,” unless there is a fit occasion to irritate purposely the judges, as was the case with Socrates.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: And you, if you are preparing such a peroration, why do you wait, why do you obey the order to submit to trial?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: When one of those who were present said, “Persuade me that logic is necessary,” he replied: Do you wish me to prove this to you?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Do you see, said Epictetus, that you yourself are admitting that logic is necessary, if without it you cannot know so much as this, whether logic is necessary or not necessary?
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: Every error comprehends contradiction: for since he who errs does not wish to err, but to be right, it is plain that he does not do what he wishes.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: But every rational soul is by nature offended at contradiction, and so long as it does not understand this contradiction, it is not hindered from doing contradictory things: but when it does understand the contradiction, it must of necessity avoid the contradiction and avoid it as much as a man must dissent from the false when he sees that a thing is false; but so long as this falsehood does not appear to him, he assents to it as to truth.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: He then is strong in argument and has the faculty of exhorting and confuting, who is able to show to each man the contradiction through which he errs and clearly to prove how he does not do that which he wishes and does that which he does not wish.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For if anyone shall show this, a man will himself withdraw from that which he does; but so long as you do not show this, do not be surprised if a man persists in his practice; for having the appearance of doing right, he does what he does.
quotes.author: Epictetus

quotes.text: For this reason Socrates also trusting to this power used to say, I am used to call no other witness of what I say, but I am always satisfied with him with whom I am discussing, and I ask him to give his opinion and call him as a witness, and though he is only one, he is sufficient in the place of all.
quotes.author: Epictetus
